appraisal_events.evidence: Discovering that the narrator knows Legrandin has no right to call himself Legrand de Méséglise and understands the real gulf between Cambremer and Guermantes, Crécy 'se sentit exister'; the narrator compares him to an old Latinist regaining confidence in life on hearing someone quote a line of Horace after the burning of all the world's libraries.
appraisal_events.explanation: Reduced to poverty and isolation, Crécy is locally restored to a sense of significance through the narrator's recognition of the arcane social knowledge that is his only remaining currency.

appraisal_events.evidence: Having absorbed Charlus's contemptuous doctrine that petty nobles like the Cambremer are no better than 'le dernier pioupiou' of a regiment, Morel snubs their first invitation by silence and a last-minute telegram, delighted with himself as though acting like a prince of the blood; later Charlus himself stands up the dinner arranged to display him to the fashionable Férés, sending only Morel with a vague excuse, and Mme de Cambremer nearly faints with disappointment.
appraisal_events.explanation: Twice the Charlus-Morel pair snubs the Cambremers' social overtures, publicly humiliating them before the guests they hoped to impress and pushing the two households toward an eventual near-total breach.

appraisal_events.evidence: Mme Verdurin corners Brichot and tells him Mme de Cambremer mocks him as 'la fable de son salon,' warning he will dishonor his old age and compromise his career, and even invokes his private domestic life; the effort succeeds, and Brichot is so wounded that he nearly loses his sight and his illness visibly worsens.
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Verdurin exercises decisive emotional and social control over Brichot, wounding him severely in order to pull him back from the Cambremers and reassert her authority over the little clan.

status_effects.explanation: Being recognized as someone for whom the social universe still exists briefly restores Crécy's sense of purpose amid his diminished, impoverished life.
The couple's efforts to draw Charlus's circle closer and display it to their own guests are twice rebuffed, undermining their standing with the little clan.
She is directly and visibly humiliated when Charlus fails to appear before the very guests, the Férés, she meant to impress with him.

The narrator frames Morel's newly borrowed aristocratic contempt as delusional self-importance, calling the application of Charlus's lessons 'burlesque' even as Morel revels in feeling like a prince of the blood.
By standing up the Cambremers' dinner and having Morel answer for him, Charlus openly demonstrates his power over the violinist and, by extension, over the Cambremers' social plans.
Devastated by Mme Verdurin's attack on his reputation and private life, Brichot is broken enough that his health and eyesight visibly decline.
Her intervention becomes 'un jour de grande émotion' for the whole little clan, publicly reasserting her dominance over a member who had begun drifting toward the Cambremers.

ambiguities: M. de Crécy shares his family name with Odette de Crécy (Mme Swann); the passage explicitly notes the two are unrelated, but the shared surface form 'Crécy' could cause mis-resolution downstream.
